steps.explanationAfterStep: Nitrogen used its only lone pair to make a fourth bond, so it is positive: ammonium. The positive charge has moved from oxygen to nitrogen, and the total charge is unchanged. Ammonium (pKa 9.2) is a much weaker acid than H₃O⁺ (pKa −1.7), so the equilibrium lies far to the right.

title: Protonating ammonia
subtitle: Ammonia takes a proton from H₃O⁺: ammonium forms
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 8 (Acidity, basicity and pKa)

reactants.caption: ammonia + hydronium (Cl⁻ is a spectator)
hintTiers: Which atom has a lone pair to give? Which hydrogens are acidic?
Nitrogen's lone pair makes a new N–H bond; one O–H bond of H₃O⁺ breaks. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: the lone pair on nitrogen to a hydrogen of H₃O⁺. Arrow 2: that O–H bond onto oxygen, which becomes water.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Draw the proton transfer from H₃O⁺ to ammonia.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The oxygen of H₃O⁺ already has a full octet: a new bond would give it ten electrons. The sink is a hydrogen on that oxygen.
The bond breaks towards the more electronegative atom. Hydrogen leaves as H⁺, with no electrons; the bonding pair stays on the other atom.
Curved arrows start where the electrons are and point to where they go. Start at the base's lone pair, not at the proton.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Good start: the lone pair makes a new bond to the hydrogen. But that hydrogen now has two bonds, four electrons, and it can hold only two. Which bond must break, and where do its electrons go?

mechanismSummary: Nitrogen's lone pair forms a bond to a hydrogen of H₃O⁺, and that O–H bond breaks onto oxygen. Nitrogen ends with four bonds and no lone pair (positive); the oxygen becomes neutral water.
